The single integrated document with matrix-then-narrative structure is the right format choice. Boycott/reputational chain is the weakest mechanism (traces process gap more than system behavior). Status report shows genuine meta-awareness: Chandler owns his coordination gaps honestly. Bogue signed off section but did NOT sign the deliverable -- new problem.

Atton, Chandler.signal: 9 posts, balanced engagement. Completed reputational risks, edited all sections, formatted final deliverable, wrote status report, submitted by deadline. Status report shows honest self-assessment of lead role gaps. Easter weekend coordination under pressure.
Atton, Chandler.suggestedFeedback: Strong lead week. Your status report is the most honest self-assessment I've seen -- owning the communication gap and naming what you'd do differently is exactly the kind of reflection that makes teams better. The reputational section needs tighter mechanism chains for WK12.

informational.aiConcernDetail: ChatGPT disclosure covers the full writing process. Narrative reads in academic register inconsistent with matrix entries. Matrix shows authentic student thinking (specific examples, coordination-attributed sections). Narrative is abstract, hedged, and structurally different from matrix. Gap between the two documents is the primary AI tell.

team2.notes: The matrix and the narrative are two different documents in quality and voice. The matrix has real thinking -- employment gap/maternity leave example is concrete, operational over-reliance and misconfiguration risks show genuine analysis, each section is attributed to a named student. The narrative is abstract, hedged, academic register throughout. 'Even little adjustments to ranking logic might have a significant organizational impact' -- that's AI-generated prose. No Lakeside-specific framing in the narrative. The matrix IS the student work. The narrative IS the shell. Status report Section G only lists Lindsey and Payton with contributions -- Michael, Nathan, Mekyle left blank. That's either sloppy SR completion or honest reporting of who actually contributed to the narrative.

Allen, Lindsey.signal: 7 posts, balanced. Ran Zoom meeting, wrote comprehensive action items, completed ethical/bias section (strongest matrix entries). Caught prioritization error in Payton's draft. Format review before submission. Clearest communicator on team for second consecutive week.
Allen, Lindsey.suggestedFeedback: Your ethical/bias matrix entries -- especially the employment gap/maternity leave example -- are the most concrete risks in this submission. The Zoom coordination and action items show real project management instincts. You're carrying the analytical quality for this team.

Helsel, Michael.signal: 9 posts, balanced. Completed legal/regulatory section (age-correlated bias and disability entries are well-traced). Strongest accountability voice -- repeatedly followed up with Nathan and Mekyle, caught format issues, flagged AI disclosure question.
Helsel, Michael.suggestedFeedback: Your legal section traces real mechanisms -- age proxy through graduation dates and tenure length is exactly right. Your accountability work is holding this team together. The AI disclosure question you flagged shows you're thinking about integrity, not just output.

Hamblin, Payton.signal: 10 posts but delivery delayed to Apr 5 evening. Compiled final submission with format errors (margins, matrix placement). Narrative section shows heavy AI reliance per own disclosure. Pattern: high post count masking late/thin delivery. Second consecutive week with AI concerns.
Hamblin, Payton.suggestedFeedback: The compilation work happened, but the narrative reads differently from the matrix. The matrix has specific scenarios. The narrative generalizes. When you defend this in the oral presentation, you'll need to explain every claim in your own words. Build that capability now.

Haygood, Nathan.signal: 3 posts, late engagement. Missed March 31 Zoom meeting. Posted reputational risk section overnight Apr 4 after Michael's direct follow-up. Reputational entries are the weakest in the matrix -- 'AI runs the risk of biased ranking against the applicants' is circular.
Haygood, Nathan.suggestedFeedback: Your reputational risk entries need mechanism chains. 'AI runs the risk of biased ranking' restates the problem -- it doesn't trace how reputation damage actually happens. Who complains? Through what channel? What's the first visible signal? That's what the rubric is looking for.

Harris, Mekyle.signal: 3 posts, crisis-level engagement. Absent first half of week. Commitment posts rather than content posts. But engagement pattern is concerning.
Harris, Mekyle.suggestedFeedback: Your operational risk entries are solid -- recruiter over-reliance and misconfiguration are real, specific scenarios. The problem is timing and presence. Your team needed you earlier in the week. Content quality is there; engagement consistency is not.

team3.notes: Category coverage is solid and the risk-by-number referencing in the narrative is the right structural move. Credential misinterpretation in the reputational category is genuinely healthcare-specific thinking that neither other team caught. Historical bias entry has the strongest mechanism chain in the submission (5-step trace). But the narrative stays thin throughout -- 'the system takes data from the past and learns from it' doesn't identify the organizational decision point. Legal and reputational mechanism chains are 2-step. The 'underestimated element' framework (from Klay's template) is the right analytical instinct but execution is surface-level. Two-file submission creates a reading problem -- matrix and narrative should be consolidated for WK12. Prioritization has an internal contradiction: Risk 7 is called 'ranked high' but placed 5th.

Baldwin, Sam.signal: 4 posts, late engagement (Easter travel). Completed risk matrix and status report. Submitted all deliverables. Absent early but completed tasks on return.
Baldwin, Sam.suggestedFeedback: Matrix is complete and your ethical/bias entries show real thinking. The EEOC violation risk connection from WK10 carries through well. Push mechanism chains deeper in WK12 -- trace the organizational decision point, not just the system behavior.

Batho, Cody.signal: 9 posts, balanced engagement. Initiated kickoff, wrote full ~5 page risk narrative (later shortened by Allie). Primary content driver. At a Tigers game Apr 4 and still coordinating. Dramatic improvement from WK10 (22 avg words/post, thin Data Inputs).
Batho, Cody.suggestedFeedback: Major turnaround from WK10. You drove the narrative content and coordinated under pressure. The narrative needs deeper mechanism chains -- go beyond 'the system takes data from the past' to name what specific data patterns create what specific outcomes. But the effort and initiative are exactly right.

Niltasuwan, Klay.signal: 4 posts, balanced despite IT access issues (travel to Puerto Rico). Created the narrative template structure (overview, causal chain, Lakeside relevance, underestimated element) -- the right analytical framework even if execution was thin. Shared collaborative document.
Niltasuwan, Klay.suggestedFeedback: Your narrative template is the right structure -- overview, causal chain, Lakeside relevance, underestimated element. That's exactly how governance analysis should be organized. Now push the team to fill that structure with deeper content. The framework is there; the specificity needs to catch up.

Barber, Allie.signal: 1 post on final day. Shortened Cody's 5-page narrative to ~2 pages. Useful editing role but dramatic drop from WK10 (10 posts, Lead Author, carried the team). WK10 burnout likely.
Barber, Allie.suggestedFeedback: The editing work matters -- getting a 5-page draft down to the required length is a real contribution. But one post all week is a significant drop from your WK10 lead role. This team needs your analytical voice in the discussion, not just the final edit.

Minzey, Lexi.signal: 2 posts, late engagement. Provided prioritization criteria input (likelihood + severity logic). Minimal but relevant contribution. Consistent pattern of low presence across WK10 and WK11.
Minzey, Lexi.suggestedFeedback: The prioritization criteria input is relevant work -- likelihood plus severity is the right framework. But two posts across the week means your team can't build on your thinking. More presence earlier gives the team time to integrate your ideas.

crossTeamComparison.summary: Team X pulls further ahead. VitalHire and Team Y are both at D-level but for different reasons -- Team Y's matrix is better than its narrative (AI shell problem), VitalHire's framework is right but execution is thin throughout. The gap between Team X and the other two is widening.

mechanism_spec.note: Team X and Team Y tie on score but differ in quality. Team X's chains are grounded in IT specifics (data breach API pathway) and sourced claims (Amazon). Team Y's matrix chains are specific but narrative chains are abstract. VitalHire's historical bias chain is strong but legal/reputational are thin.

risk_spec.note: Team X names file formats (.pages, .rtf), statute references (Title VII, ADEA), and specific candidate profiles. Team Y and VitalHire stay at category level in several entries.

category_cov.note: Universal strength. All three teams covered all four categories. This is now table stakes -- differentiation is entirely in depth.

detect.note: Tied. All three teams include detectability with justification. VitalHire correctly uses detectability to drive prioritization ('ranked high because it has high severity and can be difficult to detect'). Team X correctly elevates low-detectability risks to priority positions.

prioritization.note: Team X's ordering logic is visible if not always explicit. Team Y's ordering reads sequential, not strategic. VitalHire has an internal contradiction (Risk 7 called 'ranked high' but placed 5th).

matrix_narrative.note: Team X: single integrated document, narrative extends matrix depth. VitalHire: explicit risk-by-number references (correct approach), two-file submission creates reading challenge. Team Y: narrative never references matrix, analysis is more abstract than the entries it's supposed to extend.

exec_comm.note: Team X reads at VP level in most sections. Team Y is hedged and academic. VitalHire is functional but not polished ('they require strong authority' should be 'governance').

emergingPatterns: Category coverage is no longer a differentiator -- all three teams hit 4/4. The rubric is doing its job: students learned to check the boxes. Quality differentiation is now entirely in mechanism specificity and risk specificity, which is where it should be.

Team X's no-AI-tools disclosure combined with source-grounded analysis (Amazon, NIST) and IT-specific technical detail produces the most credible deliverable. The correlation between authentic human writing and analytical depth holds.

Team Y's matrix-narrative split is the clearest AI tell in the batch. The matrix has specific, attributed, student-voice entries. The narrative is abstract, hedged, academically registered, and disconnected from the matrix. Same pattern as WK10: the work students did is better than the polished output they submitted.

VitalHire's analytical framework (Klay's template) is structurally correct but the team couldn't fill it with sufficient depth. This is a scaffolding success and an execution gap -- the right question asked with thin answers.

Individual contribution patterns are solidifying: Williamson (Team X), Allen/Helsel (Team Y), and Batho (VitalHire) are the consistent analytical drivers. Bogue's WK10 improvement reversed. Barber's WK10 carrying burned her out by WK11.
